newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel faces tough public sell in Bundesbank clash.
newsitem.headline: Waigel faces tough public sell in Bundesbank clash.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday faced the precarious situation of winning public support for his controversial plan to revalue Germany's gold reserves after the Bundesbank on Wednesday rejected the plan.

German politicians and the press poured hefty criticism on Waigel and the government for planning to override the respected German central bank and revalue its gold reserves to help Bonn qualify for Europe's single currency.
The Frankfurt-based central bank late on Wednesday issued a statement strongly rejecting Waigel's plan, which demanded an immediate payout of the profit booked from the hidden reserves.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) demanded that Waigel resign after his unprecedented clash with the central bank.

A Bundesbank council member and SPD party member, Ernst Welteke, also warned Chancellor Helmut Kohl he had failed to win public support for his pet project and that the Bundesbank would command more public sympathy than politicians in a clash.
"Politicians do not have a great deal of credit with the public at the moment," Welteke said in an interview late on Wednesday with German radio.
"The people's trust that the transition period from the deutschemark to the euro can be a stability-oriented one lies much more with the Bundesbank than with politicians," he said.

Financial experts also denounced the grab for gold as a threat to the euro currency Bonn wants to dearly launch on schedule on January 1, 1999 and said Waigel's plan undermined the credibility of the future currency.

"The Bundesbank statement represents a huge slap in the face for Waigel and sets the stage for an open conflict with the government," said Holger Fahrinkrug, an economist at Union Bank of Switzerland in Frankfurt.
German financial markets got a small scare from the clash.
The dollar surged more than a pfennig against the mark in European dealings and German debt prices slumped in London trade since the Frankfurt market was closed for a holiday.

Nations seeking to enter European Monetary Union must, among other factors in the Maastricht Treaty, have a 1997 budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Bonn's deficit figure for 1996 was 3.8 percent, and without the 20 billion marks gained from the reserves there appears to be little chance Germany will qualify for EMU.
But the Bundesbank's Welteke, like other many newspaper commentaries, expressed an undertone of resignation that the central bank cannot prevent the reserves revaluation.
Kohl has the majority in Bonn to change the bank's laws to do it, and he made clear on Tuesday evening he would use his political power to get his way.

"The government's behaviour endangers what we need most urgently - international credibility," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told Thursday's Berliner Zeitung. He called on Waigel to quit, saying: "The man is no longer tolerable".

Saxony state premier Kurt Biedenkopf, a member of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), said Bonn should back down. Going ahead, he said, "means we won't have the authority we need to defend the independence of a European Central Bank".
Commentators warned the gold plan was a high-risk gamble that threatened to destroy Germany's reputation for responsible economic policy, a hallmark of its dramatic post-war recovery.

"The government and the Bundesbank are on a confrontation course with an uncertain outcome," saud Germany's biggest newspaper, the popular Bild daily. "But one thing is sure -- there will be more than one bloody nose in this fight."

It said Germany's high-handed insistence that other Europeans refrain from budgetary tricks to qualify for EMU would now come back to haunt Bonn as it revalues the reserves to get a badly needed injection of cash.
"Bonn's obnoxious and loud insistence about the need for discipline will now come back to haunt it. It will be a painful awakening," the newspaper said.
